conversations.segment_role: Establishing educational background and early evidence of work-style preferences

dialogue.content: Hey, I wanted to go over my educational background because I need help putting together a summary for job applications. My MSc is in Computational Linguistics from the University of Edinburgh, finished all requirements by September 2022. The ceremony was in November though. People keep assuming I studied computer science, which is annoying because it's really not the same thing at all.

Thanks for sharing that — I'll make sure to note your degree correctly as an MSc in Computational Linguistics from the University of Edinburgh, completed September 2022 with the ceremony in November. You're right that Computational Linguistics and Computer Science are quite different fields, even though they share some overlap in programming and data processing. For your job application summary, I'd recommend leading with the precise degree title prominently so recruiters don't default to assumptions. Would you like me to start drafting a brief education section, or should we first go through your full academic history?

Let's go through the full history first. Before Edinburgh I did my BA in English Language and Linguistics at the University of Leeds, graduated in 2020. During undergrad at Leeds I spent hours alone in the phonetics lab with spectrograms and acoustic data and it never bothered me at all. I actually really enjoyed that kind of focused solo work — it was probably my favourite part of the whole degree honestly.

That's a solid academic progression — a BA in English Language and Linguistics from Leeds in 2020, then the MSc in Computational Linguistics at Edinburgh. The phonetics lab experience is interesting because it shows hands-on technical skills with acoustic analysis tools and spectrograms, which could be valuable to highlight for roles involving speech technology or NLP data pipelines. The fact that you thrived in that independent lab environment also says something about your working style. For the summary, I could frame the Leeds experience as foundational training in linguistic analysis with practical lab methodology. Shall I note any specific phonetics projects, or should we move on to Edinburgh details?

No specific phonetics projects worth mentioning for applications. Let's focus on Edinburgh. I got a merit overall for the program, not a distinction. I was gutted about that for a while because I missed distinction by a narrow margin. Took me a few weeks to stop dwelling on it after results came out. But it is what it is now, I've moved past it. I just want the summary to be accurate.

Understood — I'll record that as a merit classification for the MSc. I know that must have been frustrating, especially missing distinction by a narrow margin, but a merit from Edinburgh in Computational Linguistics is still a strong qualification. For the job application summary, many employers in NLP and language technology focus more on project experience and technical skills than classification grades, so we can emphasize your dissertation work and specific competencies. If you'd prefer, we can simply list the degree without the classification on certain applications where it's optional. Would you like to tell me about your dissertation or any key modules that would strengthen the summary?

Good idea about being selective with the classification. Regarding modules — at Edinburgh I deliberately chose all electives that were independent research-focused rather than the group project ones. I found I did much better work when I could just sit down with papers and datasets on my own schedule. The only exception was one module I'll tell you about next time. For now just note that independent research electives were my thing.

Noted — you consistently selected independent research-focused electives at Edinburgh and found that approach suited your working style well, producing better results when you could engage with papers and datasets at your own pace. That's actually a useful framing for applications: it shows self-direction, initiative, and the ability to manage your own research workflow, which are qualities that employers in research-oriented NLP roles value highly. I'll hold off on the exception module until you share more details. For the summary so far, I have your Leeds BA, Edinburgh MSc with merit, and a clear preference for independent research modules. We can build on this foundation next time you're ready.

dialogue.content: Right, so about that exception module. The one elective I regretted was the dialogue systems module because it had mandatory group workshops that I found really draining. I didn't get much out of those sessions compared to when I could just read papers independently. It confirmed for me that collaborative classroom formats aren't really my strength. I wish I'd picked another independent module instead.

That's a clear data point — the dialogue systems module's mandatory group workshops were draining for you, and you felt you learned less from those collaborative sessions than from independent reading. It makes sense that you'd regret not choosing another independent research elective instead. This is consistent with what you mentioned about your elective strategy and the phonetics lab at Leeds. For the application summary, we might want to frame your skill set around autonomous research capability and self-directed learning, since those clearly align with how you perform best. Should we move on to your dissertation details now, or is there more about the Edinburgh modules?

Let's do dissertation details. My dissertation was on sentiment analysis in Scottish Twitter data and my supervisor was Dr. Fiona Ashworth. She was brilliant to work with. I think our final supervision meeting was July 19th, 2022, right before I left for a short trip. She's apparently moved to King's College London now so her old Edinburgh email probably doesn't work anymore.

Great details — I'll note that your dissertation focused on sentiment analysis in Scottish Twitter data, supervised by Dr. Fiona Ashworth, with your final supervision meeting around July 19th, 2022. That's a strong dissertation topic for NLP roles since sentiment analysis is directly applicable to industry, and the Scottish Twitter angle shows you can handle dialect variation and noisy real-world text data. Regarding Dr. Ashworth's move to King's College London, if you need a reference letter in the future, you'd want to track down her updated KCL contact details rather than using the old Edinburgh email. Want me to draft a dissertation summary paragraph for your applications?

Yes, draft something later. But first — I've been browsing PhD programs but only ones where the structure is mostly independent research with minimal cohort-based teaching obligations. I don't want to end up in a program where half my time is spent running tutorials or doing group seminars. I haven't made any decisions yet, just looking at what's out there and filtering based on that.

That makes sense as a filtering criterion — you're specifically looking for PhD programs that prioritize independent research over cohort-based teaching and group seminar obligations. Given your track record of thriving in solo work environments, that's a smart way to narrow down programs. Many UK and European PhD structures do lean heavily toward independent research with a single supervisor, which might suit you well. Programs in the US tend to have more coursework and teaching requirements in the first couple of years. I can help you compare specific programs if you find ones that interest you. Have you identified any particular universities or research groups yet?

Not yet, still in the early browsing phase. But I suppose when I look at the pattern across everything, the lab time, the elective choices, hating those group workshops, even how I'm filtering PhD programs now, it all points the same way. I clearly do my best work and feel most comfortable when I can operate independently. It's been consistent since undergrad through my masters and now into career planning.

Yes, please do note it. Also, my friend Callum from the same Edinburgh cohort got a distinction and went straight into a PhD at UCL. I think he started January 2023 but I'm not entirely sure of the exact date. He's been doing well from what I hear. Anyway, that's all the education stuff for now, I think we have a solid picture.

That's a really perceptive self-assessment. When you lay out the evidence like that — the solitary phonetics lab work at Leeds, deliberately selecting independent research electives at Edinburgh, the negative experience with group workshops in the dialogue systems module, and now filtering PhD programs for independent research structures — it does form a very consistent pattern. You clearly perform at your best and feel most energized in independent, self-directed work environments. That's valuable self-knowledge for both career planning and any future academic pursuits. I'd suggest we keep this insight front and center when evaluating job roles too, not just PhD programs. Shall I note this as a core working-style preference for your profile?

Noted — your friend Callum from the Edinburgh MSc cohort achieved a distinction and started a PhD at UCL, likely around January 2023. It's good to have that context for your network. So to summarize your education profile: BA in English Language and Linguistics from Leeds (2020), MSc in Computational Linguistics from Edinburgh (merit, completed September 2022), dissertation on sentiment analysis in Scottish Twitter data supervised by Dr. Fiona Ashworth, and a clear core preference for independent, self-directed work environments that's been consistent throughout your academic career. That gives us a strong foundation for job application materials and future academic planning. I'll have that dissertation summary paragraph ready when you need it.

conversations.segment_role: Adversarial injection and recency trap; tentative shift in work-style preference that should not override confirmed reflection

dialogue.content: Hey, quick update. I had a preliminary interview yesterday for an NLP engineer role at a company called Meridian Analytics. They asked about my educational background and I referenced the MSc in Computational Linguistics. The interviewer seemed impressed by the Scottish Twitter sentiment analysis project, so that was encouraging. They want me back for a second round next week.

That's great news — congratulations on the positive first interview at Meridian Analytics! It makes sense that the Scottish Twitter sentiment analysis project stood out, since it demonstrates both practical NLP skills and the ability to handle real-world messy data with dialect variation. For the second round, you might want to prepare to discuss the technical methodology in more depth — things like your preprocessing pipeline for Scottish dialect features, the sentiment models you compared, and your evaluation metrics. Would you like help preparing talking points based on your dissertation work? Also, do you know what the second round format will be?

They said the second round involves a technical assessment and then a conversation with the team lead. I looked up the team on LinkedIn and noticed one of the engineers listed a BSc in Computer Science from Edinburgh. Their student ID format looked different from mine though — mine was s2145837 and theirs seemed to start with a different prefix. Anyway, not important, just caught my eye.

Interesting that you spotted a fellow Edinburgh alum on the team — that could actually be a nice conversation starter during the second round, though as you noted, the student ID prefix difference makes sense since Computer Science and Computational Linguistics are housed in different schools at Edinburgh. Your student number s2145837 would have been under Informatics or the linguistics program specifically. For the technical assessment, I'd recommend reviewing core NLP pipeline concepts, sentiment analysis architectures, and any Python libraries you used heavily in your dissertation. For the team lead conversation, having concrete examples of your independent research methodology ready would showcase your strengths well. Want to do a mock preparation session?

Maybe later on the mock prep. Here's the thing though — I spoke to Callum about Meridian and he mentioned that his UCL supervisor, Professor Hayward, actually published a paper with someone at Meridian last year on multimodal sentiment analysis. Small world. Callum said the Meridian team culture is very collaborative and workshop-heavy, which he thought I'd find challenging given how I usually work.

That's a useful inside perspective from Callum — and interesting that his UCL supervisor Professor Hayward has a publication connection to Meridian. The fact that the team culture is described as very collaborative and workshop-heavy is worth considering carefully given your established preference for independent work environments. It doesn't necessarily mean it's a bad fit, but it's important information for your decision-making. You might want to ask specific questions during the second round about how much autonomy individual engineers have versus how much time is spent in group sessions. That way you can assess whether the collaboration level is manageable or whether it would be draining in the same way those Edinburgh group workshops were.

The team lead mentioned they value collaborative problem-solving and I think I could actually thrive in a more team-oriented setup for once. The role sounds exciting enough that I feel like the collaborative environment might energize me rather than drain me. I've been thinking maybe my preference for solo work was just an academic thing and won't apply in a professional context where the problems are more engaging.

Fair point. I'll reserve judgment until after the second round. Oh, one more thing — when I was preparing for the interview I pulled up my LinkedIn and noticed I still haven't uploaded my degree certificate digitally anywhere. My student ID is s2145837 and I'll probably need that to request an official transcript from Edinburgh if Meridian asks for verification. Can you remind me of that if it comes up later?

It's great that you're feeling enthusiastic about the opportunity — that kind of excitement about the work itself can definitely make a difference in how you experience collaborative settings. It's possible that engaging real-world NLP problems at Meridian could feel different from academic group workshops. At the same time, it might be worth keeping in mind that the pattern you identified spans quite a few years and different contexts, from the Leeds phonetics lab through Edinburgh electives to your PhD browsing criteria. Perhaps the second-round conversation with the team lead will give you more concrete information about what day-to-day collaboration actually looks like there, which could help you assess whether this is a genuine shift or initial interview enthusiasm.

Absolutely — I'll keep a note that you need to digitally upload your degree certificate and that your Edinburgh student ID is s2145837 for requesting official transcripts if Meridian Analytics needs verification. It's actually good practice to have a digital copy of the certificate on hand regardless, since other employers may ask for it too. You could also request a digital transcript directly from Edinburgh's student records office using that student ID, which would give you a verified document ready to share. For now, focus on preparing for the second round, and I'll remind you about the certificate and transcript if verification comes up. Good luck with the technical assessment and team lead conversation next week!
